newsitem.title: UK: Med crude market sees relief in Iraq news, eventual.
newsitem.headline: Med crude market sees relief in Iraq news, eventual.

text.p: Mediterranean crude buyers saw eventual relief from high sour prices in news Iraq may resume exports within 10 days, but doubt lingered as to how quickly Kirkuk barrels would really come on stream.
Iraqi oil minister Amir Rasheed's statement in Madrid that exports under the renewed oil-for-food deal with the United Nations would restart soon caused a volte-face in market sentiment.
One seller of Russian Urals crude, the main regional competitor for Iraqi barrels, predicted his prices would tumble by 50 cents immediately and by $1 over the next two weeks.

The news also put in stark contrast two rumoured Urals sales on Tuesday morning at dated Brent -80 cents. The deals could not be confirmed but the talk underlined the strong demand for Urals before the Iraqi news came out.

Syrian term contract negotiations were also thrown into turmoil, with the dated Brent -55 cents repeatedly requested by Sytrol now looking much too expensive, buyers said, particularly for deliveries in the second half of July.
The Iraqi news came out just after the July loading programme for Urals crude, which scheduled delivery of 2.8 million barrels of sour from the Black Sea port of Novorossiisk.

Traders said demand had built so strongly during the period from June 8, when the Iraq deal was rolled over, to today's announcement, that most Urals cargoes in the first half of July were already committed.
"It will be interesting to see what prices those cargoes fetch when they are re-offered," said one dealer, "that is the first test of where the market has fallen to."
Traders warned that a tight shipping market, Iraq's need to secure contracts with buyers and bureaucratic delays in securing U.N. approval may push back the arrival of the Iraqi barrels to mid-July.
"People are short sour on a prompt basis and with most of the first half of Urals gone already they are going to have to pay to cover themselves," said one trader.
He saw Urals prices sticking around dated Brent -$1.00/0.95 until it was clear when Iraqi barrels would become available.
However when Iraq does resume shipments the effect on crude prices may be severely depressive.
As values fall Iraq will have to ship more to reach its six-month $2 billion U.N.-limit on sales.
It is also unclear how U.N. resolutions allow Baghdad to stagger sales in the remainder of the six-month period, raising the prospect of a glut of oil deliveries over the summer.
West African grades were stronger on Tuesday, with the thin Brent/Dubai spread continuing to make them attractive in Asia, where buying has been heavy.
"I reckon there is only a quarter of the July cargoes left. The East is still looking and if the U.S. wants any Nigerian barrels it will have to pay up, and quickly," said one trader.
A third decade July Forcados was heard traded on Monday at dated Brent +23 cents, and a Bonny Light for dated Brent +42-45 cents between the same two counter-parties, but this could not be confirmed.
Brass river was on offer at dated Brent +50 cents, traders said, up from a rumoured deal at the end of last week in the high 40's over the benchmark crude.
